questions.question: When should you use git merge versus git rebase in a Java backend project?
questions.title: Git merge vs rebase — when to use each
questions.direct_answer: Use merge to preserve the full history of parallel development and for integrating long-lived feature branches into main. Use rebase to produce a cleaner, linear commit history on short-lived topic branches before merging, or to keep a feature branch up-to-date with main without introducing merge commits.
questions.interviewer_intent: Assesses understanding of Git history management, team workflow conventions, and the trade-offs between readability and traceability in collaborative Java projects.

sections.title: Two Ways to Integrate Work — and Why History Shape Matters at 2 AM
sections.content:
Every Git team eventually fights about this: merge or rebase? The debate feels religious, but the real decision is structural — it determines what `git log` looks like and how you investigate production incidents.

**Merge** creates a new commit that joins two branch tips, preserving every commit in its original form and maintaining the full directed acyclic graph of parallel development. When you look at history, you see exactly when two lines of work converged. **Rebase** replays your commits on top of a new base, rewriting SHA hashes to produce a clean linear sequence — as if the work happened in order on a single branch.

The consequence shows up during an incident at 2 AM. Merge history lets you pinpoint exactly when a feature was integrated — the merge commit maps to a specific PR and review. Linear rebase history makes `git bisect` faster because there are no merge commits confusing the binary search. Neither is universally better; your team's deployment model, compliance requirements, and review workflow determine which shape serves you.

The golden rule that prevents disasters: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a branch someone else has pulled. Violating this forces teammates into `git reset --hard` recovery — and in a busy Java backend team, that means lost work.

sections.title: The Core Trade-offs: Merge vs Rebase Side by Side
sections.content:
The differences are not just cosmetic — they affect safety, tooling, and team workflows in concrete ways.

| Dimension | git merge | git rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History shape | Non-linear DAG with merge commits | Linear chain of commits |
| Original SHAs preserved | Yes — nothing is rewritten | No — every replayed commit gets a new hash |
| Safe on shared branches | Always safe — adds a commit | Dangerous — requires force-push |
| Conflict resolution | Resolved once at merge time | May need resolution per replayed commit |
| `git bisect` friendliness | Merge commits can confuse the search | Clean linear history is ideal for bisect |
| Audit trail | Exact record of when branches converged | Looks clean but the timeline is synthetic |
| CI/CD integration | Merge commit is a natural deployment gate | Requires discipline to not rebase after push |
| Ideal use case | Integrating completed features into main | Cleaning up a feature branch before PR |

sections.title: The Decision Framework: Match the Tool to the Branch Lifecycle
sections.content:
The decision comes down to two questions: is this branch shared, and what story does the team need from history?

For **integrating completed features into main**, merge is almost always correct. The merge commit becomes a clear milestone — one commit that maps to one pull request, one code review, one deployment decision. This is especially valuable in regulated Java backend environments where audit trails matter. If something breaks in production, `git log --merges` gives you the timeline of every integration event.

For **keeping a feature branch current** during active development, rebase onto main daily. This produces a clean diff for reviewers and avoids the noise of upstream merge commits cluttering your branch. But stop rebasing the moment someone else pulls your branch.

The **squash-and-merge hybrid** is increasingly popular in microservice teams. Each PR collapses into a single commit on main regardless of how many WIP commits existed during development. You get the cleanest possible main history at the cost of losing individual commit attribution within a feature. Configure GitHub to append the PR number (`#123`) in the squash commit message so the detailed history remains accessible through the PR page.

The trap teams fall into: debating merge vs rebase on every PR instead of encoding the decision in branch protection rules. Pick a convention, enforce it with CI gates, and stop relitigating during code review.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Merge preserves the full DAG with original SHAs** — creates a merge commit recording exactly when branches converged, giving audit-quality history for incident review and compliance traceability
- **Rebase rewrites every replayed commit's SHA** — produces linear history ideal for `git bisect`, but breaks references anyone else holds to the original commits
- **Never rebase a pushed shared branch** — teammates who pulled the old history face diverged refs and must `git reset --hard`, which risks lost uncommitted work across the team
- **`--force-with-lease` is the safety net** — unlike `--force`, it checks that the remote branch hasn't moved since your last fetch, preventing silent overwrites of a teammate's emergency hotfix
- **Squash-and-merge is the modern hybrid** — each PR collapses into one commit on main giving clean history, but loses per-commit attribution; append the PR number in the message to preserve traceability

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Merge and rebase both integrate changes from one branch into another — the code result is identical. The difference is entirely in what `git log` looks like afterward and whether history is ever rewritten.

**Merge — preserving honest history**
- Merge creates a merge commit that records exactly when the feature branch entered the main branch — during an incident, that bookmark tells you which commit introduced a change and when
- Fast-forward merges skip the merge commit when the branch is linear, but the default `--no-ff` flag keeps it, making integrations visible in the graph
- Merge never rewrites pushed history, which makes it safe to use on any shared branch without coordinating with teammates

**Rebase — rewriting for a cleaner story**
- Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a linear history as though the feature was developed after all main-branch changes — reviewers see purposeful commits, not tangled WIP entries mixed with upstream merges
- The critical rule: never rebase a branch that others have checked out — replaying commits produces new SHAs, and a force-push after rebase silently overwrites any commits your teammates added on top of the old SHAs
- Use `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force` when pushing after a rebase — it checks that no one pushed to the remote branch while you were rebasing and fails safely if they did

**Squash-and-merge — the practical compromise**
- Squash-and-merge collapses the entire PR into one commit on main, attaching the PR number — you get linear history without the discipline of clean individual commits throughout development
- The trade-off: `git bisect` and `git blame` become less precise since the full development history is collapsed; for a PR that touched ten files it can be harder to isolate which change introduced a bug

Pick one convention, encode it in branch protection rules, and stop re-deciding it in every code review.

questions.question: How does Git Flow compare to trunk-based development, and which suits a Java backend team?
questions.title: Git flow vs trunk-based development
questions.direct_answer: Git Flow structures work around long-lived branches (feature, develop, release, hotfix, main) and suits teams with scheduled release cycles. Trunk-based development has everyone integrate into a single main branch multiple times per day using feature flags and short-lived branches, enabling continuous delivery. Most modern Java backend teams with CI/CD pipelines favor trunk-based development.
questions.interviewer_intent: Probes knowledge of branching strategies, CI/CD maturity, and the ability to align version control practices with deployment frequency and team size.

sections.title: The Real Question: Can Your Team Ship from main Every Day?
sections.content:
Git Flow was designed in 2010 for a world where software shipped in versioned releases with explicit freeze periods. It prescribes a strict branch topology — `develop` accumulates features, `release/*` branches stabilize them, `hotfix/*` patches production, and `main` holds only released code. **Trunk-based development** (TBD) flips this entirely: all developers integrate into a single trunk multiple times per day, hiding incomplete work behind feature flags rather than branches.

The choice is not academic — it determines your deployment frequency, merge conflict rate, and CI pipeline architecture. Git Flow's extra branches create ceremony that protects against half-baked releases but slows velocity. Trunk-based development eliminates that ceremony in exchange for demanding a fast, reliable test suite and disciplined feature flagging. Without those prerequisites, TBD just means deploying broken code.

In practice, the decision comes down to whether your Spring services can ship from `main` daily. If your CI runs in under 15 minutes and your team has feature flag infrastructure, trunk-based is the natural choice. If you must freeze `release/*` branches for contractual drops or maintain multiple supported versions simultaneously, Git Flow's structure still earns its complexity.

sections.title: Git Flow vs Trunk-Based: Where They Actually Differ
sections.content:
The comparison reveals that the strategies optimize for fundamentally different deployment models — scheduled releases versus continuous delivery.

| Dimension | Git Flow | Trunk-Based Development |
|---|---|---|
| Long-lived branches | develop, release/*, hotfix/* | Only main — feature branches live 1–2 days max |
| Release cadence | Scheduled / versioned releases | Deploy on every merge to main |
| Feature flags required | No — branches hide incomplete work | Essential — in-progress code is on main |
| CI pipeline complexity | Must run on multiple long-lived branches | Single integration point simplifies CI |
| Merge conflict risk | High — branches diverge over days/weeks | Low — small, frequent integrations |
| Hotfix process | Dedicated hotfix branch merged to main + develop | Patch main directly, redeploy immediately |
| Team onboarding | More rules and branch types to learn | Simpler mental model, fewer ceremonies |

sections.title: The CI/CD Pipeline Shape Changes With Your Branching Model
sections.content:
Misalignment between branching strategy and pipeline architecture is one of the most common sources of deployment friction in Java backend teams. The branching model dictates how your pipeline must be structured.

For **trunk-based development**, the pipeline is straightforward: every merge to `main` triggers build, test, and deploy to staging. Promotion to production uses a manual approval gate or a canary deployment that auto-promotes after health checks pass. The pipeline must be fast — under 15 minutes for build and test combined — because it runs on every merge. Invest in Gradle build cache, test parallelization, and selective test execution that only runs tests affected by changed modules.

For **Git Flow**, the pipeline fans out across branches. The `develop` branch deploys to a dev environment, `release/*` branches deploy to staging with full regression suites, and merges to `main` deploy to production. The hidden cost is the **hotfix dual-merge problem**: a hotfix branch must merge to both `main` and `develop`. Forgetting the `develop` merge means the fix disappears on the next release cut. Automate this with a GitHub Action that creates a PR to `develop` whenever a hotfix merges to `main`.

The pragmatic middle ground most Java teams land on is **scaled trunk-based**: short-lived feature branches (one to two days) merged via PR after a green CI build. This gives you the code-review gate without weeks-long branch divergence.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Git Flow optimizes for versioned, scheduled releases** — the `develop` / `release/*` / `hotfix/*` topology makes sense when you must freeze code, run week-long QA cycles, or support multiple deployed versions simultaneously
- **Trunk-based optimizes for continuous delivery** — everyone integrates into `main` frequently, hiding incomplete work behind feature flags; this demands a fast test suite (under 15 minutes) or you're deploying broken code
- **Git Flow's hidden cost is the hotfix dual-merge** — a hotfix must merge to both `main` and `develop`; forgetting the `develop` merge means the fix vanishes on the next release cut, a silent regression
- **Merge conflict risk scales with branch age** — Git Flow branches diverge for days or weeks, making Java refactors across packages painful; trunk-based keeps diffs small and merge conflicts rare
- **Scaled trunk-based is the pragmatic middle** — short-lived feature branches (1–2 days) plus protected `main` gives review gates without Git Flow's heavyweight topology

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Git Flow and trunk-based development are both valid branching strategies — the right choice depends on how your team ships and whether you must maintain multiple deployed versions simultaneously.

**Git Flow — structured release management**
- Git Flow works around two long-lived branches: `main` holds production code and `develop` accumulates features; release branches stabilize a version before it merges to main
- Built for teams that ship versioned releases on a schedule — the `release/*` branch gives a freeze window for QA without blocking new feature work on `develop`
- The hotfix dual-merge trap catches most teams eventually: a `hotfix/*` branch must merge to both `main` and `develop`; skip the `develop` merge and the fix silently disappears when the next release is cut

**Trunk-based development — continuous integration as a practice**
- Everyone integrates small, complete changes to main (or a short-lived branch measured in hours) — the merge conflict rate drops because branches diverge for a day, not weeks
- Incomplete features hide behind feature flags rather than long-lived branches, which decouples deployment from release — you ship code to production before the feature is user-facing
- Requires a fast CI pipeline and a culture of green builds; a broken main blocks everyone, so the feedback loop must be short enough that developers fix it immediately

**How to choose**
- Trunk-based is the right default for most Java backend teams: fewer conflicts, faster integration, and a forcing function for small commits
- Git Flow is justified when the team contractually supports multiple deployed versions — B2B SaaS customers on staggered upgrade schedules, libraries that maintain multiple minor version branches

Invest in feature flag infrastructure before adopting trunk-based — it is the mechanism that makes incomplete features safe to deploy.

questions.question: How do you resolve merge conflicts effectively in a Java backend codebase?
questions.title: How to resolve merge conflicts effectively
questions.direct_answer: Resolve merge conflicts by first understanding both sides of the change, using a three-way diff tool to compare ancestor, ours, and theirs, then making a deliberate editorial decision. In Java codebases, the most common conflicts occur in import blocks, dependency files (pom.xml/build.gradle), and auto-generated sources. Automated pre-merge practices — rebasing frequently and keeping PRs small — reduce conflict frequency dramatically.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests practical day-to-day Git proficiency, communication skills around collaboration, and knowledge of tooling available for Java projects.

sections.title: Why Understanding Intent Matters More Than Picking a Side
sections.content:
A merge conflict is not an error — it is Git telling you that two humans made decisions about the same code, and a third human (you) needs to make the editorial call. The mistake most developers make is treating conflicts as an annoyance to dismiss quickly: accept mine, accept theirs, done. That reflex silently drops features, introduces duplicate logic, or creates compile errors that only surface in CI twenty minutes later.

The real skill is **reading intent before touching markers**. A conflict in `UserService.java` means nothing without knowing that one branch added OAuth support while the other refactored session management. Blindly picking one side deletes the other feature entirely. Java codebases have specific conflict hotspots that make this worse: auto-sorted import blocks produce spurious conflicts, `pom.xml` version strings collide when two branches bump different dependencies, and Lombok-generated code creates diffs in files nobody actually edited.

The three-way merge view — showing the common ancestor alongside both branches — is the single most important tool. It turns an ambiguous two-way diff into a clear picture of what each side intended to change relative to the original.

sections.title: Read Both Sides Before Editing Any Marker
sections.content:
Before opening the conflicted file, run `git log --merge -p <file>` to see the commits from both branches that touched this file. Read the commit messages — they explain *why* each change was made. A conflict between "add retry logic to payment call" and "extract payment call to separate service" requires combining both changes, not picking one.

In **IntelliJ IDEA**, use the built-in three-way merge dialog (Git → Resolve Conflicts). It shows the common ancestor in the center, your version on the left, their version on the right, and lets you cherry-pick hunks from either side into the result. This is dramatically more effective than reading raw `<<<<<<<` markers in a text editor, especially for Java files where the conflict spans method boundaries.

For `pom.xml` dependency conflicts, don't arbitrarily pick one version. Check Maven Central for the newest compatible version of the dependency. If both branches bumped different libraries, you likely need both changes — take the union of additions. The test in the next step will catch any incompatibilities immediately.

sections.title: Compile and Test Immediately — Don't Trust Your Edit
sections.content:
After resolving every conflicted file, run `mvn compile` or `./gradlew compileJava` before doing anything else. This catches two classes of problems instantly: stray **conflict markers** (`<<<<<<<`) that cause cryptic parse errors, and broken imports from missing or duplicate lines that Java's strict compilation rules will flag immediately.

Then run the test suite: `mvn test`. A merge resolution that compiles but breaks a test is worse than one that fails to compile — the compile failure is obvious, but a silent behavioral regression can reach production. Pay special attention to tests that exercise the code paths modified by *both* branches, since that is exactly where your editorial decision could have been wrong.

Once tests pass, stage with `git add <files>` and commit with `git commit`. Git pre-populates the merge message describing which branches were merged. Augment it with a note about non-trivial resolutions: "Resolved UserService conflict by combining OAuth support from feature/auth with session refactor from feature/sessions." Future engineers reading `git blame` will thank you for that context.

sections.title: Prevent Conflicts Before They Happen
sections.content:
The best conflict resolution strategy is reducing conflict frequency. Two practices cut conflict rates by roughly 80% in busy Java backend teams.

First, **rebase your feature branch onto main daily** rather than waiting until merge time. A one-day divergence produces small, manageable conflicts. A one-week divergence produces cascading conflicts across files where the context has shifted so much that the three-way merge loses its usefulness.

Second, **keep PRs under 400 lines of change**. Large PRs touch more files, increasing the probability of overlap with concurrent work. A PR that changes 50 files has a near-certain chance of conflicting with someone else's work on a team of ten. A PR that changes 5 files rarely conflicts.

For Java-specific sources of spurious conflicts, configure consistent import ordering via `.editorconfig` or Checkstyle rules so the formatter never produces diffs in import blocks. Use `.gitattributes` with `merge=union` for purely additive files like `CHANGELOG.md` where both sides' additions are always valid. For `pom.xml` version conflicts, centralize dependency versions in a `<dependencyManagement>` block in a parent POM — branches that add dependencies reference the managed version rather than specifying their own, eliminating the most common source of XML merge conflicts.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Read intent before resolving markers** — `git log --merge -p <file>` plus commit messages explain why both sides touched the same code; blindly accepting one side silently drops the other feature
- **Three-way merge is the essential tool** — IntelliJ's ancestor + ours + theirs view makes `pom.xml` and service-layer conflicts legible; raw marker editing in a text editor is error-prone
- **Compile immediately after resolution** — `mvn compile` catches stray `<<<<<<<` markers and broken imports in seconds, before they waste 20 minutes in CI
- **Rebase daily, PR under 400 lines** — one-day divergence produces small conflicts; one-week divergence produces cascading conflicts where context has shifted beyond three-way merge usefulness
- **`.gitattributes merge=union` for additive files** — eliminates spurious conflicts in changelogs and other append-only files where both sides' additions are always valid

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A merge conflict means two branches modified the same code in incompatible ways. The instinct to immediately edit conflict markers is the wrong first move — understanding why both sides touched the same code tells you which changes should survive.

**Understanding the conflict before editing**
- Run `git log --merge` before touching conflict markers to see which commits on each side modified the conflicting files — a conflict in a service class often means two features changed the same method, and blindly picking one side silently deletes the other
- Three-way merge tools (IntelliJ's merge dialog, VS Code's diff editor) show the common ancestor alongside both branches — resolving hunks individually is safer than picking entire sides wholesale
- For `pom.xml` conflicts, always resolve manually — take the union of both additions and verify compatibility against Maven Central; automated tools often discard one team's dependency silently

**After resolving — verification before committing**
- Run `mvn compile` immediately after resolving Java file conflicts — stray conflict markers cause cryptic parse errors, and broken imports from duplicate lines fail compilation before they waste test time
- Run the full test suite before pushing the resolution — a conflict resolution that compiles but breaks tests has introduced a regression under the appearance of a clean merge
- Use `git diff HEAD` to review what the final resolved state looks like as a whole before committing — conflicts in multiple files can interact in non-obvious ways

**Prevention — the best conflict is the one that never happens**
- Rebase onto main daily during active development to minimize divergence; PRs under 400 lines conflict far less often than large PRs
- Enforce consistent import ordering via Checkstyle or Spotless so the formatter never produces spurious diffs in import blocks that cause false conflicts
- Communicate intent before making large structural refactors — a team-wide rename or package reorganization should be a coordinated commit, not a PR that collides with everyone else's work

questions.question: When backporting a bug fix to a maintenance branch, should you use cherry-pick, merge, or rebase?
questions.title: Cherry-pick vs merge vs rebase for backporting fixes
questions.direct_answer: Cherry-pick is almost always the right tool for backporting: it copies one or more specific commits to a target branch without bringing along unrelated changes. Merge would pull in the entire branch history, and rebase would replay all commits since the divergence point — both are too broad for a targeted backport. Reserve merge and rebase for integrating full feature work.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests knowledge of selective change propagation, maintenance branch management, and the real-world scenario of supporting multiple deployed versions of a Java service.

sections.title: Backporting Needs a Scalpel, Not a Sledgehammer
sections.content:
Backporting means taking a fix from the main development line and applying it to an older release branch still running in production. Java services in enterprises commonly run multiple concurrent versions — a `v2.x` branch on long-term support while `v3.x` carries active development. The challenge is applying *only* the fix without dragging along months of unrelated features.

This is where the three Git propagation tools — **cherry-pick**, **merge**, and **rebase** — diverge sharply. Cherry-pick copies specific commits to a target branch without touching anything else. Merge pulls in the entire source branch history since divergence. Rebase replays every commit since the branches split, rewriting SHAs along the way. For a targeted backport, only cherry-pick gives you the surgical precision needed.

The common mistake is reaching for merge out of habit. Merge works beautifully for integrating completed features, but when you merge `main` into `v2.x`, you pull in every commit since the branch point — three months of new features dumped into what is supposed to be a stable, minimal maintenance release. That violates the entire purpose of a maintenance branch.

sections.title: Cherry-pick vs Merge vs Rebase for Targeted Backports
sections.content:
Each tool propagates changes differently, and the differences are consequential when maintaining stable release branches alongside active development.

| Dimension | cherry-pick | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Selectivity | Copies specific commits only | Brings entire branch history | Replays all commits since divergence |
| SHA preservation | New SHA on target branch | No rewrite — merge commit added | Rewrites all replayed SHAs |
| Safe on shared branch | Yes — only adds commits | Yes | No — requires force-push |
| Risk of pulling in unrelated features | None — only selected commits travel | High — entire source branch merged | High — all commits replayed |
| Audit traceability | Use `-x` flag to record source SHA | Merge commit links both histories | No automatic link to original |
| Automation support | GitHub/GitLab backport bots available | Manual process | Manual process |

sections.title: The Cherry-pick Workflow: From Fix to Backport in Three Commands
sections.content:
The practical workflow for backporting a security fix from `main` to `release/2.x` starts with identifying the **exact commit SHA** on main that contains the fix. Use `git log --oneline main` or find the merge commit of the PR that delivered the fix.

Switch to the maintenance branch and cherry-pick with the `-x` flag. The `-x` flag appends the source SHA to the commit message, creating an audit trail that links the backport to its origin.

```bash
git checkout release/2.x
git cherry-pick -x abc1234
# -x appends "(cherry picked from commit abc1234)" to the message
```

This **traceability** is critical in regulated industries — fintech, healthcare, government — where you need to prove that a CVE fix was applied to every supported release. The `-x` annotation in the commit message creates that audit trail without any additional tooling.

If the cherry-pick conflicts because the surrounding code has diverged on the maintenance branch, resolve the conflict manually. Sometimes the fix depends on a refactor that only exists on main. In that case, you have two options: cherry-pick the refactor commit first (in order), or write a standalone fix specifically for the `v2.x` code context. The standalone fix is usually safer because it avoids pulling in refactoring assumptions that may not hold on the older branch.

After resolving, run the full test suite against the maintenance branch to verify the fix works in the older codebase context — dependencies, APIs, and framework versions may differ from main.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cherry-pick is surgical** — copies selected commits to another branch without dragging unrelated mainline history; the only appropriate tool for backporting CVE fixes to `release/2.x`
- **Merge backports the whole branch** — merging `main` into a maintenance branch pulls every commit since divergence, dumping months of new features into a stable release and violating its purpose
- **Rebase is never the right backport tool** — it replays the entire commit range since divergence and rewrites SHAs, forcing a disruptive force-push on a shared maintenance branch
- **`-x` flag creates an audit breadcrumb** — appends the original SHA to the cherry-picked commit message so compliance teams can trace a security patch across every supported release branch
- **Dependency chains require ordered cherry-picks** — if a fix depends on a refactor absent from the old branch, cherry-pick both in order or write a standalone fix for the older code context

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Backporting a bug fix to a maintenance branch requires copying a specific commit without bringing along unrelated history. Cherry-pick is the right tool for this — the other two options bring far more than you want.

**Cherry-pick — surgical backporting**
- `git cherry-pick -x <sha>` copies one specific commit to the current branch and appends the original SHA to the commit message — the `-x` creates a traceable link from the maintenance branch commit back to the main-branch source
- Cherry-pick is correct when the fix is a single, well-scoped commit on main; if the fix spans multiple commits, cherry-pick them in order so the branch compiles at each step
- When the target branch diverges enough that the patch does not apply cleanly, write a standalone fix for the older context rather than importing assumptions from main that do not hold there

**Why not merge for backporting**
- Merging `main` into `v2.x` brings three months of new features, API changes, and dependency upgrades along with the one security fix — the maintenance branch loses its purpose of being a stable, minimal surface
- Merge commits also obscure what was actually ported, making audit trails harder to produce for security teams

**Why not rebase for backporting**
- Rebase replays every commit since the branch diverged — on a maintenance branch that split six months ago, that could be hundreds of commits replayed onto a codebase with different structure
- Rebase rewrites SHAs and requires a force-push on a shared branch that other engineers have checked out

The key enabling practice: keeping commits on main small and logically cohesive. A fix committed alongside a refactor cannot be cherry-picked cleanly. Teams that commit features as single atomic units spend far less time on backport conflicts.
